brief.reader: Platform or SRE engineer who runs OpenTelemetry Collectors in front of Splunk Observability Cloud and owns what reaches it
brief.question: Customer tokens show up in our trace URLs and health checks fill our traces. Can the Collector fix both before the data reaches Splunk, without losing real traces, and does naming the URL attributes cover every place the token lands?

demand.evidence: open-telemetry/semantic-conventions issue 860 'Http client and server span default collection behavior for url.full and url.query attributes' (open since 29 Mar 2024; 6 reactions, 24 comments) and issue 128 'Semantic conventions vs GDPR' (20 comments); Splunk docs 'Manage sensitive data in Splunk Observability Cloud' (instrumentation must scrub sensitive values before setting url.query, url.path, url.full); guides people use, with their wording: OneUptime 'Drop Kubernetes Liveness and Readiness Probe Spans with OTTL' (10 Sep 2026), OneUptime 'Redact Passwords, Tokens, and URL Secrets with OTTL Patterns' (10 Sep 2026), Dash0 'Redacting Sensitive Data in the OpenTelemetry Collector' (updated 15 Jul 2026), Better Stack 'Redacting Sensitive Data with the OpenTelemetry Collector'. Phrases: 'drop health check spans', 'redact query parameters', 'mask token in URL', 'probe spans'. News: OTTL v1 in contrib v0.164.0 (The New Stack, Oct 2026); transform processor stable graduation proposed 18 Nov 2026 (collector-contrib 53322).

brief.decision: Whether to clean trace data in the Collector with OTTL, now that OTTL is stable: which spans to drop, which values to mask, and whether naming the URL attributes is enough
brief.takeaway: OTTL in a gateway Collector (contrib 0.165.0, where OTTL is stable) can drop the kubelet's health-check spans and mask a customer token before anything reaches Splunk, while the sample traces keep their 3 spans and both services (20 of 20 per run is the target). Measured on EKS with zero-code Python services emitting old and new HTTP attribute names: masking two named attributes (url.query, url.full) versus every attribute value, read back from Splunk APM trace by trace, with the attributes that still hold the token named, and health checks counted in APM and in the services' own metrics.
brief.open_question: On EKS with two zero-code Python services that pass a customer token in the query string and emit both current and older HTTP attribute names, behind a gateway Collector contrib 0.165.0: with batch only, with a filter plus replace_pattern on url.query and url.full, and with the same filter plus replace_all_patterns on every attribute value, two runs each of 45 s at 10 orders a second, how many spans of 20 sample traces per run in Splunk APM hold the raw token and in which attributes, how many hold the masked value, do traces keep all 3 spans and both services, and how many /healthz requests do APM and the services' HTTP metric count per config over the same 10 s points?

brief.adds: The OTTL, transform and filter processor docs and vendor guides (Dash0, Better Stack, OneUptime) show redaction and health-check statements one at a time, and Splunk's docs ask instrumentation to scrub sensitive query values, but none measures end to end what reaches Splunk. This lab runs three gateway configs on EKS with real zero-code services emitting old and new HTTP names and real kubelet checks, reads each sample trace back from Splunk APM by its ID, names the attributes that still hold the token, and counts health checks in APM and in the services' metrics per config.
tradeoffs: Naming url.query and url.full misses the older http.target and http.url the same spans carry during a semantic-convention migration; masking every attribute value covers both but runs the pattern on every attribute
Dropping health-check spans removes them from traces only; the services' HTTP metrics still count them, and a slow health check no longer shows in a trace
A gateway Collector is one more hop to run; the agent could run the same processors
The OTTL language is stable, while the transform processor is beta and the filter processor alpha, which matters for adoption
One token name in the query string, one load level and one gateway; a token in a header, a body or a span event needs its own statement
